new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngamo (both Gudi and Yaya dialects) is described as a two-level tone language (H, L; falling HL contour, rare rising LH) with contrastive vowel length; in Gudi every lexical tone pattern has shifted one tonal domain rightward (Great Ngamo Tone Shift) leaving default L initially and floating final tones. None of the first-hand descriptions (Schuh 2005, 2009; Schuh et al. 2009; Grubic 2015) says anything about word stress or accentual prominence, positive or negative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: proper names, ideophones, some recent Hausa/Bole loans resist the GNTS; Yaya has downstepped H.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical citation forms and phrase-level tone rules within the intonational phrase (Schuh 2009 §3-5); TBU is the mora (Schuh 2005:5). No word-stress domain is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern first-hand material (Schuh 2005/2009, Schuh et al. 2009, Grubic 2015) is primarily on the Gudi dialect of Ngamo (Gadaka area), with comparative data from the Yaya dialect; Schuh and Ibriszimow both note the two dialects differ enough in phonology (especially tone, because of the Gudi-only Great Ngamo Tone Shift) to border on separate languages. Glottolog ngam1282 covers both; no separate glottocodes for Gudi/Yaya are known to me.

new_statements.quote: - stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter [p. 6] ... All Chadic languages are tone languages, i.e. relative voice pitch on individual syllables is part of the lexical representation of words ... Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang (and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies), but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties. [p. 89] ... Ngamo has a two-tone system with downdrift. [p. 133]
new_statements.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2017. A Chadic Cornucopia (ed. Paul Newman). eScholarship, University of California (UCLA Linguistics).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted fragments verified verbatim with extracted text at the stated locators: PDF p. 25 (printed p. 6, ch. 1 book outline, item '5. Tones and Intonation'): '- stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter'; PDF p. 108 (printed p. 89, ch. 5 sec. 1): 'All Chadic languages are tone languages, i.e. relative voice pitch on individual syllables is part of the lexical representation of words.. Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang (and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies), but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, s…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Schuh et al. 2009 dictionary: Ngamo is a tone language, no stress statement). Schuh 2017 adds an explicit statement that stress is not a prosodic parameter, but at the FAMILY level ('no Chadic language'), not in the Ngamo-specific sections; the Ngamo sections (ch. 5 sec. 6; ch. 8) restate the two-tone system with downdrift, contrastive vowel length and the Gudi Great Ngamo Tone Shift and say nothing about stress. The catalog record's empty rule can be filled as 'tonal; stress not a prosodic parameter (family-level statement, Schuh 2017 pp. 6, 89)'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngamo is a two-tone (H/L) language with downdrift and contrastive vowel length; falling tone is restricted to monosyllables or word-/utterance-final syllables in Gudi. The only statement on stress is family-wide: no Chadic language (hence Ngamo) has stress as a prosodic parameter; whatever prominence is heard is a by-product of tone, syllable weight and intonation. No Ngamo-specific stress rule is given because the author holds there is none to give.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ngamo. Schuh notes that Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang have treated stress as distinctive, but he does not accept stress as a prosodic parameter anywhere in Chadic. Ch. 4 (Phonotactics, Syllables, Syllable Weight, pp. 86-88) is only an unwritten outline; its Ngamo entry mentions syllable-weight polarity and dislike of geminates, nothing on stress. a full-text search for stress/accent the book: the only 'stress' hits are the two family-level passages, bibliography titles, and a non-phonological 'laying stress on'.
new_statements.identity_note: The Cornucopia's Ngamo data are mainly from the Gudi dialect (Jibir Audu Janga Dole, Umaru Mamu Goge) with Yaya comparison (Isa Adamu Gashinge); ch. 5 sec. 6 treats both Gudi and Yaya Ngamo (Great Ngamo Tone Shift in Gudi), ch. 8 focuses on Gudi. Both dialects fall under ngam1282. The stress statement itself is about the Chadic family as a whole, quantified over 'all/no Chadic language'.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2009. Ngamo tones and clitics. Ms., UCLA, 46 pp. (retrieved via the Internet Archive from www.linguistics.ucla.edu/people/schuh/Papers/)

sources.note: Nothing about stress/accent. Fullest description of Gudi (and briefly Yaya) Ngamo tone: two tones H/L, falling and rare rising contours, floating H diagnostics, downstep in Yaya, tone rules within the intonational phrase, clitic tones.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2005. The Great Ngamo Tone Shift. Ms., UCLA (second revision, July 2005), 31 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Entirely about tone: Gudi Ngamo shifted every lexical tone one tonal domain to the right with default L on the initial domain; TBU = mora; H/L (+F, rare R) system; floating tones. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur only for diacritics (grave/acute accent). Notes syllable weight (light/heavy, one extra-heavy syllable) but no prominence statement.
